annotations.keyFindings: Across four homes, 71 percent of residents were reviewed within six months and 58 percent of recommendations were implemented within four weeks; mean regular medicines fell from 9.4 to 8.1.
annotations.limitations: Stepped introduction without concurrent control; secular change possible.

annotations.keyFindings: Rounds lasted where a named deputy and a fixed monthly slot existed; they stopped in two of five homes after the pharmacist left.
annotations.limitations: Five homes; observers were part of the programme.

annotations.keyFindings: Families took part in 23 percent of reviews; acceptance of recommendations was 74 percent with family involvement against 52 percent without.
annotations.limitations: Acceptance recorded at the review, not at follow-up.

annotations.keyFindings: 21 controlled studies: fewer regular medicines; imprecise and inconsistent effects on falls and mortality; restarts rarely reported.
annotations.limitations: Most included studies at high risk of bias.
annotations.notes: Supports not claiming effects on falls.

annotations.keyFindings: A checklist completion index scored eight core steps; mean completion 78 percent; goals of care and action owners most often missed.
annotations.notes: Usable fidelity measure from round notes.

annotations.keyFindings: Across 22 homes, adoption ranged from 30 to 90 percent of scheduled reviews; homes with electronic records reached more residents; short-stay residents were reached least.

claims.text: In a stepped introduction across four homes, 71 percent of residents were reviewed within six months and 58 percent of recommendations were implemented.
claims.passage: 71 percent of residents were reviewed at least once within six months of rounds starting, and 58 percent of the recommendations made were implemented within four weeks
claims.interpretation: Planning values for reach and for implementation of recommendations.

claims.text: Rounds were sustained where a named deputy could lead them and a fixed monthly slot was protected, and stopped in two of five homes after the pharmacist left.
claims.passage: Rounds were sustained in homes where a named deputy could lead them and a fixed monthly slot was protected, and they stopped in two of five homes after the pharmacist left.
claims.interpretation: Build a deputy and a fixed slot into each home's rounds.

claims.text: Deprescribing interventions in long-term care reduced regular medicines, while effects on falls and mortality were imprecise and inconsistent.
claims.passage: Interventions reduced the number of regular medicines, but effects on falls and mortality were imprecise and inconsistent.
claims.interpretation: Track falls as a balancing measure without claiming benefit.

claims.text: Recommendations were accepted more often when a family member took part (74 percent) than when none was involved (52 percent).
claims.passage: Recommendations were accepted more often when a family member took part (74 percent) than when no family member was involved (52 percent).
claims.interpretation: Invite families and record their participation.

synthesis: Six retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Interdisciplinary rounds in comparable homes reached most residents within six months and led to most recommendations being implemented, but sustainability depended on a named deputy and a protected monthly slot. Family participation was associated with higher acceptance. A systematic review shows fewer medicines with deprescribing but no clear effect on falls or mortality, so clinical outcomes should be tracked, not claimed. Routine data can measure reach and adoption, and a checklist completion index can measure fidelity from round notes.
gradeRationale: Uncontrolled and observational implementation studies with consistent findings on reach and sustainability; the clinical effect evidence is low certainty and imprecise.
summary: Six records appraised; four source-derived claims; certainty low.
